concepts.title: Ordered Pairs and Their Equality
concepts.definition: An ordered pair records two objects in a fixed sequence, so swapping the slots generally produces a different pair; two ordered pairs match only when both slots agree one by one.
concepts.formula: a = c and b = d when (a, b) = (c, d)
concepts.key_idea: Match first slots with first slots and second with second to read off unknowns.

concepts.title: Cartesian Product and Its Size
concepts.definition: The Cartesian product of two sets strings out every possible ordered pair with the first slot drawn from one set and the second from the other; its element count is the product of the two counts, and the order of the product matters.
concepts.key_idea: Every element of A teams with every element of B; multiplying the sizes counts the teams.

concepts.title: Counting Subsets and Relations of a Product
concepts.definition: Every relation from A to B is a subcollection of the pairs in A x B, so the number of possible relations equals the number of subsets of A x B, obtained by doubling once per pair.
concepts.key_idea: Count the pairs first, then double that many times for the subset total.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_004_relations.txt, section 4.4 note: total relations from A to B are 2^pq; illustration n(A) = 3 gives 2^9

solution_steps.action: multiply the set sizes
solution_steps.explain: the product set holds p times q pairs

solution_steps.action: raise two to the pair count
solution_steps.explain: each pair is in or out of a relation, doubling the options

concepts.title: Relations with Domain, Range and Co-domain
concepts.definition: A relation from A to B picks out some of the pairs of A x B through a stated condition; the first slots actually used form the domain, the second slots form the range, and the whole target set B stands by as the co-domain.
concepts.key_idea: The range can never spill outside the co-domain.

concepts.title: Reflexive, Symmetric, Transitive and Equivalence Relations
concepts.definition: A relation on a set is reflexive when every element pairs with itself, symmetric when every pair can be reversed, and transitive when two chained pairs imply the shortcut pair; a relation holding all three traits is an equivalence relation.
concepts.key_idea: Test three habits in order: self-pairs, reversibility, and chain-closing.

solution_steps.action: check that (a, a) belongs to R for each element
solution_steps.explain: a single missing self-pair kills reflexivity

solution_steps.action: reverse an arbitrary pair and test membership
solution_steps.explain: one counterexample destroys symmetry

solution_steps.action: chain two pairs and test the shortcut
solution_steps.explain: transitivity needs (a, c) whenever (a, b) and (b, c) both hold

solution_steps.action: declare equivalence only when all three pass
solution_steps.explain: the three properties together define an equivalence relation

concepts.title: Functions as Unique-Image Relations
concepts.definition: A function is a relation that deals every domain element exactly one partner: nobody in the domain may be left without an image, and no domain element may split its image between two targets.
concepts.formula: function = one image per domain element
concepts.key_idea: Two failures to watch: an empty arrow and a forked arrow from the same domain point.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_004_relations.txt, Functions part, arrow diagram examples with R = {(2,1),(3,2),(4,1),(5,2),(3,3)}
question_patterns: is R = {(2, 1), (3, 2), (4, 1), (5, 2), (3, 3)} a function from its domain to its range

solution_steps.action: list the distinct first elements of the relation
solution_steps.explain: these are the domain candidates

solution_steps.action: check each first element has at least one partner
solution_steps.explain: a missing image disqualifies the relation

solution_steps.action: check no first element has two partners
solution_steps.explain: a forked image disqualifies the relation

solution_steps.action: call it a function only if both checks pass
solution_steps.explain: unique image for every domain element

concepts.title: Domain and Range of Simple Real Functions
concepts.definition: For a formula-defined function, the domain collects every real input that keeps the formula meaningful, while the range collects the outputs actually produced; squaring accepts all reals and never outputs a negative, and reciprocals refuse zero.
concepts.key_idea: Ban inputs that divide by zero; watch which outputs the rule can actually reach.

solution_steps.action: scan the formula for forbidden operations
solution_steps.explain: division by zero or square roots of negatives restrict inputs

solution_steps.action: collect the permitted real inputs
solution_steps.explain: this set is the domain

solution_steps.action: describe the outputs the rule can produce
solution_steps.explain: this set is the range
